settings.editor:
A high water bill can be frustrating, especially when nothing about your daily routine has changed. You are using the same showers, sinks, toilets, dishwasher, and washing machine, but the bill still climbs. When that happens, one of the first things to consider is a hidden plumbing leak.

Not all leaks are obvious. In many North Carolina homes, they show up quietly as a damp crawl space, a soft patch of yard, a toilet that refills when no one has flushed, or a musty smell near a cabinet or bathroom wall. A small leak may not look urgent at first, but over time it can waste water, increase utility costs, and damage floors, walls, foundations, or plumbing lines.

The good news is that homeowners can often spot early clues before the problem becomes a plumbing emergency. This guide explains why water bills rise unexpectedly, how to check for hidden leaks, and when it makes sense to bring in a professional.

settings.title: Quick Answer: Why Is My Water Bill So High?

settings.editor:
If your water bill increased suddenly and your household usage has not changed, a hidden leak is one of the most likely causes. According to EPA WaterSense, common household leaks often come from worn toilet flappers, dripping faucets, and leaking valves, which can waste thousands of gallons per year.

Common sources include:

  • Running toilets
  • Dripping faucets or showerheads
  • Leaking supply lines
  • Irrigation system leaks
  • Crawl space plumbing leaks
  • Underground water line leaks
  • Slab leaks
  • Pipe leaks behind walls or under floors

A simple first step is to turn off every water fixture and check your water meter. If the meter continues moving, water may be escaping somewhere in the plumbing system.

settings.title: First, Rule Out Normal Water Usage Changes

settings.editor:
Before assuming there is a leak, think through any recent changes that could explain the higher bill.
Water use can increase because of:

  • Guests staying at the home
  • More laundry than usual
  • Lawn watering or irrigation use
  • Filling a pool or hot tub
  • A new appliance
  • Children home during school breaks
    Outdoor hose use
    If one of these applies, the bill may reflect temporary usage. If nothing has changed, it is time to look more closely for hidden leaks.

settings.title: Try This Simple Water Meter Test

settings.editor: Your water meter can help confirm whether water is moving when it should not be.
Make sure every faucet, shower, toilet, appliance, hose bib, and irrigation system is off. Do not run the dishwasher or washing machine during the test.
Write down the number or take a clear photo with your phone.

settings.title: Step 3: Wait One to Two Hours

settings.editor: Avoid using any water during this time.
If the number changed, water is likely flowing somewhere in the system.
This test will not locate the leak, but it can tell you whether a closer inspection is needed.

settings.title: Common Hidden Leaks That Raise Water Bills

settings.editor:
A running toilet is one of the most common reasons for a high water bill. The leak may be caused by a worn flapper, faulty fill valve, or misadjusted chain.

The tricky part is that toilet leaks are not always loud. Some toilets refill quietly throughout the day, wasting water without an obvious sound.

A simple dye test can help. Put a few drops of food coloring in the toilet tank and wait 10 to 15 minutes without flushing. If color appears in the bowl, water is leaking from the tank into the bowl.

A slow drip may seem minor, but it can add up over time. Faucet and showerhead leaks are often caused by worn washers, cartridges, seals, or valves.

These leaks are usually easier to fix early, before water damages cabinets, flooring, or wall surfaces. EPA WaterSense also recommends periodically inspecting faucets and aerators as part of routine fixture maintenance.

Many homes across Central and Eastern North Carolina have crawl spaces, which means plumbing leaks can happen in areas homeowners rarely check.

Signs may include:

  • Musty odors
  • Damp insulation
  • Soft or wet soil
  • Higher indoor humidity
  • Sagging insulation near plumbing lines

Because crawl spaces are out of sight, these leaks can continue for weeks or months before they are found.

Your main water service line runs from the meter to the house. If that line leaks, you may not see water indoors at all.

Possible signs include:

  • Low water pressure
  • Wet or soft spots in the yard
  • One unusually green patch of grass
  • Water pooling near the meter
  • A meter that moves when all fixtures are off

These leaks often require professional leak detection because the pipe is buried.

If your home has a sprinkler system, irrigation leaks can cause a major bill increase. Broken sprinkler heads, cracked underground lines, and stuck valves can waste water quickly. NC DEQ notes that landscape irrigation can account for a large share of total water use, which is why broken sprinkler heads, stuck valves, or cracked irrigation lines can affect bills quickly.

Because irrigation systems often run early in the morning, leaks may go unnoticed unless you inspect the yard while the system is operating.

A slab leak occurs beneath a concrete foundation. These leaks can be harder to detect, but they should not be ignored.

Warning signs include:

  • Warm spots on flooring
  • Damp floors
  • Cracks in flooring or walls
  • Mold or mildew odors
  • Water bill increases with no visible leak

Slab leaks can affect flooring, foundation materials, and indoor air quality if left unresolved.

Some clues deserve faster attention because they may point to ongoing water damage.

Watch for:

  • Water stains that spread
  • Warped flooring
  • Soft drywall
  • Peeling paint or bubbling walls
  • Musty odors near cabinets or bathrooms
  • Low water pressure
  • Unexplained puddles in the yard
  • Mold growth near plumbing fixtures

A high bill is frustrating, but visible moisture damage is a stronger warning sign that the leak may already be affecting the home.

A small leak does not always stay small. As moisture continues, damage can spread beyond the plumbing system.

Finding the leak early usually gives homeowners more repair options and helps prevent larger damage.

It makes sense to call a plumbing professional if:

  • Your meter moves when all water is off
  • Your bill keeps rising for no clear reason
  • You see water stains, soft flooring, or mold
  • You suspect a slab or underground leak
  • You have low water pressure throughout the home
  • You cannot find the source of the problem

A plumber can use tools such as pressure testing, moisture meters, acoustic listening equipment, and camera inspections to narrow down the leak without unnecessary guesswork.

settings.title: A Practical Next Step for North Carolina Homeowners

settings.editor:
A high water bill is not always a plumbing emergency, but it is worth investigating. Start by reviewing your recent water use, then perform a meter test. After that, check toilets, faucets, crawl spaces, irrigation systems, and damp areas around the home.

If the source is not obvious, or if the meter shows water moving when everything is off, it is time to get help.
